Missouri property tax is assessed and collected at the local level, and owners can appeal an assessment.

What the official sources say

  • An appeal must be filed with the county Board of Equalization by the second Monday in July. (Paying Property Taxes Under Protest And/Or Appeal Options | State Tax Commission; source)
  • A Complaint for Review of Assessment must be filed with the State Tax Commission by September 30 of the year of assessment or within 30 days of the Board of Equalization decision, whichever is later. (File An Appeal | Missouri State Tax Commission; source)
  • Property taxes are due no later than December 31; the owner may appeal even if taxes are unpaid, or pay the full bill by December 31 marked 'paid under protest'. (Paying Property Taxes Under Protest And/Or Appeal Options | State Tax Commission; source)
  • Real property is assessed at percentages of true value: 19% for subclass (1) (residential), 12% for subclass (2) (agricultural), 32% for subclass (3) (commercial). (RSMo 137.115; source)
  • In a first class charter county or a city not within a county, at an STC or court appeal the assessor may not advocate a valuation higher than the value finally determined by the assessor or the board of equalization, whichever is higher. (RSMo 138.060; source)
  • Delinquent tax sales are held on the fourth Monday in August of each year. (RSMo 140.150; source)
  • The owner, lienholder, occupant or other interested person may redeem within one year of the sale by paying the purchase price, costs, interest per the certificate (not above 10% annually), and later taxes paid with 8% interest; the right to redeem is defeasible until the purchaser acquires the deed. (RSMo 140.340; source)

What the official sources say

  • The Missouri Property Tax Credit Claim ('circuit breaker') gives credit to certain senior citizens and 100 percent disabled individuals for a portion of real estate taxes or rent paid. (Property Tax Credit | Missouri Department of Revenue; source)
  • The credit is a maximum of $750 for renters and $1,100 for owners who owned and occupied their home, based on taxes or rent paid and total household income. (Property Tax Credit | Missouri Department of Revenue; source)
  • A county authorized to impose a property tax may grant a homestead property tax credit to eligible owners age 62 or older (owner of record of a homestead). (RSMo 137.1050; source)
Selling in Missouri?

Does Missouri have a homestead exemption?

Missouri homeowners meet three separate things that people often lump together under the homestead name: a state income-based property tax credit, a county option credit for owners 62 and older, and a creditor protection under RSMo 513.475 that shields part of a home's value from judgment collection.

Which of the three matters depends on whether the question is a tax bill, a lender or judgment creditor, or a sale. Each has its own agency, its own form and its own eligibility test, so it helps to sort them before filing anything.

What is the Missouri Property Tax Credit Claim?

It is the state's "circuit breaker," run by the Department of Revenue. The credit goes to certain senior citizens and to individuals who are 100 percent disabled, covering part of the real estate tax or rent paid for the year. The maximum is $750 for renters and $1,100 for owners who owned and occupied their home.

The department's frequently asked questions set household income caps that vary with ownership and filing status. Owners who occupied the home all year must be at $30,000 or less if single, or $34,000 or less if married filing combined. Renters and part-year owners face lower caps of $27,200 single and $29,200 married filing combined. Household income is broad: it adds Social Security, pensions, public assistance, child support and similar receipts to Missouri adjusted income.

How do I claim the credit?

The route depends on whether a Missouri income tax return is required. Filers use Form MO-1040 with the Property Tax Schedule (MO-PTS) attached, and anyone not required to file uses the stand-alone Form MO-PTC. The department says a claim for a past year can still be filed for three years after its original due date, while the 2025 claim was due April 15, 2026.

  • Bring the paid real estate tax receipt from the county collector.
  • Add every W-2 and 1099, and benefit letters where they apply.
  • Include Form 948 from the assessor if the property has more than five acres, since the credit counts the tax on five acres and the home.
  • Claim a tax bill in the year you paid it. A 2025 bill paid in 2026 goes on the 2025 claim.

The credit applies only to a home the claimant occupies, and only where property tax is actually paid on it. Sewer lateral charges, penalties and interest do not count.

What is the Missouri homestead tax credit for owners 62 and older?

It is a county option. RSMo 137.1050 lets a county that can levy a property tax grant a credit to residents who are at least 62, are owners of record or hold a legal or equitable interest shown in a written instrument, and are liable for the tax on a home they occupy as their primary residence. A county turns the credit on by ordinance or by a vote after a petition signed by at least five percent of the registered voters who voted in the last governor's race.

The credit equals the amount by which the owner's real property tax has risen since the owner's initial credit year. If new construction is added to the home, or the home is annexed into a new taxing district, the starting amount is raised to match. The county collector shows the credit on the tax statement, and the county tells each political subdivision the total by November 30 each year. To find out whether your county has adopted it, ask the county collector or assessor.

How does Missouri assess a home for tax purposes?

Residential real property is assessed at nineteen percent of true value in money, according to RSMo 137.115. Agricultural land is assessed at twelve percent, and commercial property at thirty-two percent. New values are set as of January 1 of each odd-numbered year and carry into the even-numbered year that follows, except for new construction.

The same statute requires a physical inspection before an assessor raises a residential parcel's value by more than fifteen percent from the last assessment, not counting new construction. The owner gets written notice and can ask, within thirty days, for an interior inspection. A drive-by does not count. An owner whose use of the property changes can ask the assessor to reclassify it.

What does the homestead creditor protection do?

RSMo 513.475 exempts a person's dwelling and the land used with it from attachment and execution, up to an aggregate value. The version of the section that takes effect on January 1, 2027 sets that value at $40,000, after a 2026 amendment. Where several owners of one homestead claim the exemption, together they cannot exceed the single total.

The section also bars either spouse from selling, mortgaging or otherwise transferring the homestead alone. A sale or mortgage is valid when husband and wife convey jointly. The statute calls a sale by one spouse alone null and void, so both spouses sign the deed when the house is their homestead.

Where do I get help with the credit paperwork?

The Department of Revenue runs a claim assistance page and answers questions at PropertyTaxCredit@dor.mo.gov. Proof of Social Security or Supplemental Security Income benefits can come from a my Social Security account online or by calling the Social Security Administration, while the SSA-1099 form still arrives by mail. The county collector holds the paid-tax receipt, and the assessor supplies Form 948 for parcels of more than five acres.

How do the Missouri home tax breaks compare?

Missouri homestead-related programs, from the Department of Revenue and the Revisor of Missouri
ProgramWho qualifiesWhat it does
Property Tax Credit ClaimCertain seniors and 100 percent disabled individuals under the income capsUp to $1,100 for owners and $750 for renters
County homestead credit (137.1050)Owner-occupants 62 or older in a county that adopted itCredit for the increase in tax since the initial credit year
Creditor homestead (513.475)Any owner who uses the home as a homesteadExempts up to $40,000 in value from execution, effective January 1, 2027
Residential assessment (137.115)All owners of residential real propertyAssessed at 19 percent of true value

How does selling a home affect these tax breaks?

A sale in the middle of a year can lower what you may claim. Anyone who owned the home for only part of the year uses the lower part-year income caps, and the credit is limited to a home the claimant occupies. Keep the settlement statement and the paid tax receipt for the year of sale, since the claim asks for the real estate tax you paid.

Ask the county collector how the tax for the year of sale will be split on the closing statement, and whether the county has adopted the credit for owners 62 and older.

More questions about Missouri Homestead Exemption

What is the Missouri property tax credit worth?

Up to $1,100 for an owner who owned and occupied the home, and up to $750 for a renter, according to the <a href="https://dor.mo.gov/taxation/individual/tax-types/property-tax-credit/">Department of Revenue</a>. The actual figure depends on tax or rent paid and total household income.

What is the income limit for the Missouri property tax credit?

For owners who lived in their home all year, $30,000 if single and $34,000 if married filing combined. Renters and part-year owners are limited to $27,200 single and $29,200 married filing combined, per the department's <a href="https://dor.mo.gov/faq/taxation/individual/property-tax-credit-claim.html">FAQ page</a>.

At what age can I get the county homestead credit?

Sixty-two. <a href="https://revisor.mo.gov/main/OneSection.aspx?section=137.1050">RSMo 137.1050</a> sets that minimum, and it applies only in a county that has adopted the credit by ordinance or vote. Ask your county collector whether yours has.

Does the homestead protection stop me from selling my house?

No. <a href="https://revisor.mo.gov/main/OneSection.aspx?section=513.475">RSMo 513.475</a> protects the home from execution up to a value cap and says spouses must convey jointly. A joint deed by husband and wife is allowed.

Can I still file for the credit after I sell the house?

The department allows a claim for a past year up to three years after its original due date. A claim covers real estate tax paid on a home you occupied, and a part-year owner uses the lower income caps.

content:
Missouri Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

Cash Home Buyers in Missouri

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Missouri Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House sale
  • Turn the Missouri Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Missouri House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Rent and possession: after demand for unpaid rent, the landlord may file a verified statement with an associate circuit judge; the clerk issues a summons to the tenant and occupants to show cause why possession should not be restored. (RSMo 535.020; source)
  • The one-month termination notice under 441.060 is not required before filing a rent-and-possession statement. (RSMo 535.020; source)
  • If the officer fails to deliver possession within seven days of delivery of the writ, the landlord may within 60 days of judgment, with law enforcement present and without breach of the peace, change locks and remove property. (RSMo 441.060; source)
  • After a foreclosure sale, the new owner must give a residential-tenant occupant notice that the sale occurred and that the occupant has not less than ten business days to vacate; no unlawful detainer action may begin within ten business days of the notice. (RSMo 534.030; source)
  • Section 534.030 states that nothing in it creates a tenancy between the new owner and the occupant. (RSMo 534.030; source)
Selling in Missouri?
We buy Missouri houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What are the steps of a Missouri eviction case?

A Missouri rent and possession case moves through five stages: a verified filing, a summons, a hearing, a judgment with a ten day window, and an officer's writ. Chapter 535 of the Missouri statutes lays out each stage, and the whole path runs through the associate circuit court of the county where the rented house sits.

A landlord who is not claiming unpaid rent follows a different path under chapter 534, the unlawful detainer statutes, which covers tenants who hold over after a lease ends, occupants after a foreclosure, and employees who stay after a job that came with housing ends (RSMo 534.030). The sections below follow the rent case, since that is the filing a rental owner sees most.

How does a landlord start the case?

By filing a statement under oath. RSMo 535.020 calls for an affidavit filed with an associate circuit judge that gives the rental terms, the rent actually due, the fact that payment was demanded and not made, and a description of the property. Local court rules may route these filings to one central location in the county, so the clerk can say where the paperwork goes.

Once the statement is in, the clerk issues a summons naming the tenant and every person occupying the home, ordering them to appear and show cause why possession should not go back to the landlord. The case is then handled under the Missouri rules of civil procedure except where chapter 535 says otherwise.

How is the tenant served and how soon is the hearing?

Service has to happen at least four days before the court date, and the court date in the summons cannot be more than twenty-one business days after the summons issues unless the landlord agrees in writing to a later date. That is the rule in RSMo 535.030.

If the tenant cannot be found, the landlord may ask for service by posting a copy of the summons and complaint on the dwelling and mailing a copy by ordinary mail, both at least ten days before the court date. A tenant served this way who does not show up can still lose possession, but the statute bars a money judgment against that tenant unless the tenant has entered an appearance.

When the tenant does appear, RSMo 535.040 has the judge set the case on the first available date. If the rent was demanded, is still unpaid, and the tenant does not tender the rent and costs in court, the judge enters judgment for possession plus the rent due and court costs.

What happens in the days after a judgment?

The tenant has ten days from judgment to ask the court to set it aside or to apply for a trial de novo, according to RSMo 535.030. Without one of those filings the judgment for possession becomes final and the tenant can be removed with no further notice. When the tenant was in default, the clerk mails a notice of that ten day window to the last known address.

  • Execution. The judge issues an execution that commands an officer to put the landlord in possession, and the officer must deliver possession within five days of receiving it (RSMo 535.040).
  • Seven day fallback. If the officer has not delivered possession seven days after the writ reached the officer, the landlord has sixty days from the judgment to act with a municipal or county officer present, without breaching the peace (RSMo 441.060).
  • Paperwork. The landlord must show the officer a true copy of the judgment and execution, get the officer's written acknowledgment, and file that acknowledgment in court within five days after taking possession.

How long does each step take in Missouri?

Time limits in a Missouri rent and possession case, from chapters 441 and 535
StepTime limitStatute
Serve summonsAt least 4 days before the court date535.030
Court date after summons issuesNo more than 21 business days, unless the landlord consents to later535.030
Posting and mailing serviceAt least 10 days before the court date535.030
Motion to set aside or trial de novo10 days from judgment535.030
Officer delivers possessionWithin 5 days of receiving the execution535.040
Landlord's fallback with law enforcementAfter 7 days from delivery of the writ, within 60 days of judgment441.060

Which Missouri cases are not rent cases?

Chapter 534 covers a holdover after a lease ends, an occupant who stays after a foreclosure, an employee who stays after housing tied to the job ends, and a person who took possession wrongfully and refuses a written demand to leave (RSMo 534.030). The remedy is an unlawful detainer action.

Occupancy is a separate topic. RSMo 441.060 presumes that a limit of two persons per bedroom is reasonable, and the limit does not apply to a child born to the tenants during the lease.

What happens to the tenant's belongings and the deposit?

Under RSMo 535.040 a landlord is not liable for goods left in the home after a court-ordered execution unless the landlord acted willfully, wantonly or maliciously. One exception applies: when an item carries a conspicuous permanent label showing it belongs to a third party, the landlord must send certified mail, return receipt requested, and give that party five business days after receipt to pick it up.

Deposits follow RSMo 535.300. A landlord may not take more than two months' rent as a deposit, has to hold it in an insured bank or credit union, and has thirty days after the tenancy ends to return it or mail an itemized list of damages along with the balance. A landlord who wrongfully withholds any part owes the tenant twice the amount withheld.

What should an owner who wants to sell a rented house do during an eviction?

Keep the case file in order and tell any buyer where the case stands. A buyer who is paying cash for a house with a pending eviction needs the filing date, the court date, and a copy of any judgment.

  • Do not change locks, remove doors or shut off utilities. Section 441.233 treats that as forcible entry and detainer.
  • Keep the demand, the affidavit, proof of service and the judgment together in one folder.
  • Ask the circuit clerk for the case number and the next court date, and share them with the title company.
  • Close on a date that follows the ten day window, since a judgment is not final before then.

If the sale closes before the case ends, the contract should say plainly who handles the case and the tenant afterward.

More questions about Missouri Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

How long does a Missouri eviction take?

The statutes set a hearing within twenty-one business days of the summons unless the landlord agrees to later, plus a ten day window after judgment and up to five days for the officer to deliver possession. Those limits come from <a href="https://revisor.mo.gov/main/OneSection.aspx?section=535.030">RSMo 535.030</a> and <a href="https://revisor.mo.gov/main/OneSection.aspx?section=535.040">RSMo 535.040</a>. Local court calendars and appeals add to the total.

Can a tenant stop an eviction by paying the rent in court?

Yes, if the rent and costs are tendered before the judge at the hearing. <a href="https://revisor.mo.gov/main/OneSection.aspx?section=535.040">RSMo 535.040</a> directs the judge to enter a possession judgment only when that payment has not been made.

What if the tenant never shows up in court?

The judge can still hear the case. When the tenant was served by posting and mailing, the landlord can win possession but the court may not grant a money judgment against a tenant in default, as <a href="https://revisor.mo.gov/main/OneSection.aspx?section=535.030">RSMo 535.030</a> provides.

Can the landlord keep the tenant's security deposit to cover unpaid rent?

Yes, to the extent reasonably necessary. <a href="https://revisor.mo.gov/main/OneSection.aspx?section=535.300">RSMo 535.300</a> lets the landlord withhold for unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear, and losses from short notice, and requires an itemized list within thirty days of the end of the tenancy.

Can a landlord do a lockout instead of going to court?

No. <a href="https://revisor.mo.gov/main/OneSection.aspx?section=441.233">RSMo 441.233</a> treats removing a tenant or the tenant's property without a court order, taking off doors or locks, or willfully cutting essential services as forcible entry and detainer.

What the official sources say

  • A deed conveying real property to a designated grantee beneficiary that expressly states it is not to take effect until the owner's death transfers the interest on death if executed and recorded with the recorder of deeds before the owner's death. (RSMo 461.025; source)
  • A beneficiary deed need not be supported by consideration or delivered to the grantee beneficiary, and may transfer to a trust regardless of revocability. (RSMo 461.025; source)
  • A beneficiary deed not recorded until after the owner's death is not invalidated if otherwise effective by law. (RSMo 461.025; source)
  • Small estate: distributees may take personal and real property without letters if the estate, less liens, debt and encumbrances, does not exceed $40,000, 30 days have passed since death and no letters application is pending. (RSMo 473.097; source)
  • Small estate affidavit is filed with the probate division clerk; a bond is required unless the court dispenses with it, and the filing fee under 483.580 is paid. (RSMo 473.097; source)
  • Distributees may establish their right to succeed to real estate by recording a copy of the affidavit and clerk's certificate with the recorder of deeds in each county where the real property sits. (RSMo 473.097; source)
